questions.q: Why did Solari's training Job keep showing Running in Kubernetes for days after the actual training work had finished?
options: A non-daemon background thread (the async image-upload thread) kept the process alive even after the main training loop returned, so the container never exited and the Job was never marked Completed
Kubernetes has a known bug that never marks any Job as Completed
The training script crashed and automatically restarted itself in an infinite loop
The cluster autoscaler refused to release the GPU nodes on purpose
questions.explain: From Kubernetes' perspective nothing was wrong -- the process simply never exited, because a non-daemon thread was still technically alive, so the Job's status stayed Running.

questions.q: What is the key distinction this case study draws between Job status and GPU utilization?
options: They are always the same signal and monitoring either one is sufficient
GPU utilization is only meaningful for inference workloads, never for training jobs
Job status cannot be observed in Kubernetes at all
A Job can show Running in Kubernetes while its GPUs are doing no real work at all -- status alone can't tell a healthy long job from a stalled one
questions.explain: Status and GPU utilization are independent signals; this case study's whole point is that watching only one of them misses a stalled job that the other would catch.

questions.q: What finally surfaced this incident at Solari?
options: A Kubernetes alert fired automatically the moment the job stalled
The ML engineer noticed immediately on Monday morning
A Thursday cloud-bill review -- four days after the job should have finished
The DCGM idle-GPU alert in this lesson, which was already running at the time
questions.explain: Neither alert from this lesson existed yet at the time of the incident -- the week's cloud-bill review is what actually caught the unfamiliar spike, days late.

questions.q: What does the TrainingGPUIdle alert rule in this lesson actually check?
options: Whether a training Job's YAML manifest contains a valid resource limit
Whether the Kubernetes API server is reachable
Whether a node has been provisioned longer than 8 hours
Whether average GPU utilization on a training node has stayed under 5% for 30 or more minutes, which suggests a job has stalled or finished without exiting
questions.explain: The alert is scoped to DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL averaged over a 30-minute window on training nodes, catching sustained low utilization regardless of what the Job's status says.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue for having both the job-duration alert and the idle-GPU alert, rather than just one?
options: Because Kubernetes requires at least two PrometheusRules per namespace

The duration alert catches 'this took too long' regardless of cause, while the utilization alert catches 'this GPU isn't doing real work' regardless of what Kubernetes' status reports -- together they cover failure modes either one alone would miss
Having two alerts halves the cost of each individual GPU
Only the duration alert is actually useful; the utilization alert is redundant
questions.explain: The two alerts watch different signals and catch different failure shapes -- together they close the gap that let this incident run four days before anyone noticed.
